titulo.texto: Fattened Dogs / Dancing Dogs of Colima

frase_gancho.texto: Round, shiny clay dogs that accompanied the dead.

puente_narrativo.texto: There were armed guardians, too. Look for a standing warrior with a helmet, a woven breastplate, and a club in his hands, who guarded the entrance to a tomb.

guion_corto.texto: These figures of red clay, polished until they shine, represent Colima dogs from about two thousand years ago. They are plump and round, with short legs, folds at the neck, and alert ears. They are called fattened dogs, meaning dogs raised to be fat. Some are vessels: they have a small tube through which liquid was poured. They were found in shaft tombs, next to the dead. There are dogs in several poses, and some wear a mask with a human face. There are two explanations: they were guides of the soul, accompanying the dead on their journey to the underworld, or they were food for that journey, because in ancient Mexico dogs were raised for eating. No one knows whether they were one or the other, or both.

guion_largo.texto:
If you saw the movie Coco, you already know the idea: a hairless dog that accompanies the dead. But it is much older. The Colima dogs are two thousand years old, and you have already seen clay dogs in the hall of the first villages.

The word xoloitzcuintle, which you probably know, comes from Nahuatl and means something like “dog of Xólotl,” the god tied to death and to the evening sky. But that name comes from a later period, and from the center of the country. In Colima we do not know what they called these dogs, or what they thought of them.

Let us look at the first explanation: the dog as a guide. Centuries later, the Mexica told that, upon dying, one had to cross a river of the underworld, and that a dog helped with the crossing. The Colima dogs perhaps express a similar idea, much earlier. A faithful companion for the longest journey.

The second explanation is less romantic, but just as real. In ancient Mexico dogs were raised to be eaten, and the Spanish chroniclers speak of fattened dogs that were sold in the markets. That is why they are called “fattened.” Perhaps these figures are also the food the dead person would need. The two ideas do not contradict each other: a dog can be a companion and a provision at the same time.

According to the Mexica, the road to Mictlán, the place of the dead, lasted four years and was full of trials: hills that crashed into each other, a wind of obsidian blades, deserts, and a great river. To cross it a dog was needed, and some sources say it had to have reddish fur. The Colima dogs are made of red clay. Coincidence? We do not know, but it is an image that sends shivers down your spine.

Look at the polish. The red clay was rubbed with a smooth stone before firing, until the surface gleamed as if it were wet. If you move close to the light, you will see that glow, which time has not erased. The potters of Colima were masters at this.

Lean in toward the dogs’ eyes: they are simple, outlined with a single incision, and yet they have an alert, almost human expression. It is the trick of good sculptors: with very few strokes, to achieve a gaze.

Some dogs wear a mask with a human face. It is thought that it would symbolize the transformation of the animal into a guiding being, someone between two worlds. It is one of the most enigmatic images in the hall.

And there are not only dogs. The potters of Colima portrayed an entire fauna: opossums, armadillos, turkeys, ducks, iguanas, fish. If you look carefully at the display cases, you will find a small zoo made of clay. It is proof of how closely they observed the world around them.

Today the xoloitzcuintle is a symbol of Mexico. It nearly disappeared in the twentieth century, but it recovered thanks to those who bred it again. As if the Colima dogs were still carrying out their task: accompanying us across the centuries.

texto.Material: Clay (ceramic), hand-modeled and polished, bright red in color
texto.Dimensions: 20 cm high x 19 cm wide x 36 cm long

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Colima dogs were just toys or pets.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They were tomb figures: guides for the journey of the dead and, perhaps, food for that journey.
